title: Spiders Touch Glue 1,000 Times a Web. Why No Sticking?
description:
Why don't spiders stick to their own webs? Only the capture spiral is sticky, and the spider's branching leg hairs, non-stick leg coating and careful footwork keep it from getting stuck.

Sources:
https://smithsonianscience.org/2012/03/fancy-footwork-and-non-stick-leg-coating-helps-spiders-not-stick-to-their-own-webs/
https://phys.org/news/2012-03-spiders-sticky-web-sites.html
https://science.howstuffworks.com/environmental/life/zoology/insects-arachnids/spider5.htm

Animated in the Watercolor Brush style.

topic: Why don't spiders stick to their own webs?
script:
Touch a spider web and you'll stick.
So how does the spider touch its glue 1,000 times a web?
First, not every thread is sticky.
The spokes and the frame are dry silk.
Only the spiral is beaded with tiny glue drops,
so the spider walks on the spokes.
But while building,
it still bumps the glue hundreds to thousands of times.
The real secret is in its legs.
They're covered in tiny branching hairs.
A glue drop only touches a few hair tips,
and slides right off.
The legs also have a non-stick coating.
When scientists washed it off,
the legs suddenly stuck way harder.
And the spider moves carefully,
peeling each foot away at just the right angle.
Dry spokes, hairy feet, and a built-in non-stick layer.
Honestly, that's kind of genius.
If a spider walked onto another spider's web,
would it get stuck?
key_facts: Orb webs have dry radial spokes and frame threads; only the capture spiral carries glue droplets
Orb weavers push against sticky lines hundreds to thousands of times while building one web (Briceno & Eberhard 2012)
Spider legs are covered in branching hairs that limit contact with glue
A non-stick chemical coating protects the legs: legs washed with hexane stuck more
Careful leg movements minimise adhesive forces
